albums.blurb: Ellington and Billy Strayhorn wrote this nine-part suite after the orchestra's 1963 State Department tour of the Middle East and South Asia and a 1964 visit to Japan, and recorded it in New York in December 1966. It was one of the last major Ellington–Strayhorn collaborations — Strayhorn died five months after the sessions — and it filters the tour's impressions through the band's own language rather than pastiche: Johnny Hodges's alto feature "Isfahan" and the clarinet birdsong of "Bluebird of Delhi" are the best-known movements. The whole record is instrumental big-band writing from the band's late golden period.
albums.reception: It won the Grammy for Best Instrumental Jazz Performance by a Large Group at the 1968 ceremony, and a 1995 remastered reissue later brought it back into print with alternate takes.

albums.blurb: Maya Delilah is a London singer, songwriter and guitarist in her mid-twenties who built an audience through guitar-led covers and a string of EPs before signing to Blue Note. The Long Way Round, released 28 March 2025 on Blue Note/Capitol, is her twelve-track full-length debut, moving between breezy soul-pop, soft funk and jazz-tinged balladry with her Stratocaster playing kept front and center.
albums.reception: Spotify named Delilah a 2025 Artist to Watch ahead of the album's release, and AllMusic's review characterized the record as emotionally resonant coffeehouse soul.

albums.blurb: Television were fixtures of the mid-70s CBGB scene in New York — they talked the club into booking rock bands in the first place — but their debut has little to do with punk's two-minute rush. Tom Verlaine and Richard Lloyd's interlocking lead guitars stretch the title track past ten minutes, closer to cool-toned improvisation than power chords. Released on Elektra in February 1977, it was the band's first of two albums before splitting in 1978, and its clean, angular guitar language became a reference point for post-punk and indie rock that followed.
albums.reception: Championed in a two-page NME rave by Nick Kent, it reached No. 28 on the UK Albums Chart and spent 13 weeks in the Top 75, while failing to reach the Billboard 200 at home.
